analogy.p: Think of cells as individual people, tissues as teams (all the nurses, all the surgeons), organs as whole buildings or departments (the hospital), organ systems as services (the whole emergency service) and the organism as the entire country's health system. Each level depends on the one below it and nothing works alone. It breaks down because people can't turn into other types of worker, whereas cells in an embryo differentiate and the cells of an organism all contain the same DNA.
analogy.t: A hospital and a health service

bullets: **Cell** = the basic building block of all living organisms.
**Tissue** = a group of cells with a similar structure and function.
**Organ** = an aggregation (collection) of tissues performing specific physiological functions.
**Organ system** = a group of organs working together to perform a particular function (for example digestion).
**Organism** = organ systems working together make the whole living thing.
The order is always smallest to largest: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.2.1 'Principles of organisation' says that **cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms**, that **a tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function**, that **organs are aggregations of tissues performing specific physiological functions**, and that **organs are organised into organ systems, which work together to form organisms**. You must be able to use these definitions and apply them to examples, especially the digestive system. Exam questions are usually short recall (1 to 2 marks) or application (2 to 4 marks).

bullets: A **muscle cell** contains many proteins that slide over each other so the cell can contract and shorten, and many mitochondria to release energy by respiration.
A **glandular cell** makes and releases (secretes) substances such as enzymes and hormones, so it has lots of ribosomes and other structures for making protein.
An **epithelial cell** forms a thin covering or lining, so it is flat and fits tightly with its neighbours.
A cell on its own cannot carry out a large-scale job such as digesting a meal; it needs to be grouped with similar cells.
Link to cell biology: the sub-cellular structures (nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes) explain how each cell does its job.
core.p: Every living organism is made of cells, and everything the organism does (respiration, making proteins, moving, reacting) is carried out by cells. In a multicellular organism such as a human, the cells are not all identical: during development they undergo **differentiation** and become **specialised** for a particular job. A specialised cell has a structure (shape and sub-cellular structures) that suits its function. This is the first step in building a large, efficient body.

bullets: **Muscular tissue** contracts to bring about movement (for example churning the stomach contents).
**Glandular tissue** makes and secretes substances such as enzymes, acid and hormones.
**Epithelial tissue** covers the inside and outside surfaces of the body and organs.
Other tissues you meet in the course include **nervous tissue**, **blood**, **xylem and phloem** in plants, and **meristem** tissue at plant growing tips.
A tissue is NOT the same as a paper tissue: always use the biological definition in exams.
core.p: A **tissue** is a group of cells with a **similar structure and function**. Because the cells are alike and next to each other, they can do the same job together on a bigger scale than a single cell could. Notice the exam wording: a tissue is made of similar cells, not of different types of cell. Different tissues are then combined in the next level up.

bullets: **Stomach**: muscular tissue churns the food and digestive juices; glandular tissue makes digestive juices (protease enzyme and hydrochloric acid); epithelial tissue covers the inside and outside surfaces.
**Heart**: cardiac muscle tissue pumps blood, connective tissue and nervous tissue support and control it.
**Leaf** (a plant organ): epidermis (protects), palisade mesophyll (photosynthesis), spongy mesophyll (gas exchange), xylem and phloem (transport).
**Lungs, liver, pancreas and brain** are further organs you meet during the course.
An organ has a specific function, such as pumping blood (heart) or making bile (liver).
core.p: An **organ** is an aggregation (a collection) of different tissues that together perform a specific **physiological function**. The key idea is that an organ contains several types of tissue, each doing a part of the job, so the organ can do something none of the tissues could do alone. Examiners often ask you to name the tissues in a named organ and say what each does.

bullets: **Digestive system**: breaks down food into small, soluble molecules and absorbs them into the blood.
**Circulatory system**: heart, blood vessels and blood transport substances around the body.
**Respiratory system**: lungs and airways exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
In plants, the **shoot system** and **root system** work together to make a whole plant.
Systems are interdependent: failure of one system (for example the heart) affects the others.
core.p: An **organ system** is a group of organs that work together to perform a particular function for the body. Organ systems then work together to form the whole **organism**. No organ works in isolation: for example the digestive system breaks food down, but the circulatory system carries the absorbed nutrients to all cells and the respiratory system supplies the oxygen needed to release energy from them.

bullets: **Epithelial tissue** lines the inside surface and covers the organ; a layer of mucus helps to protect the wall from the acid.
**Glandular tissue** makes and secretes hydrochloric acid and protease enzymes into the stomach lumen.
**Muscular tissue** contracts and relaxes to churn the food and mix it with the digestive juices.
The three tissues are different (different cell types), which is why the stomach is an organ and not a tissue.
The stomach is connected to the oesophagus (food in) and the small intestine (partly digested food out).
The acid gives the right conditions for stomach protease and kills many microorganisms in food.
In an exam, name the tissue, then its job, then say how it helps the organ digest food.
core.h: The stomach: where each tissue is in its wall
core.p: The stomach is the textbook organ because its wall shows three different tissues arranged in layers, each with a different job. Looking from the inside (the lumen, where the food sits) outwards, the surface is covered by **epithelial tissue** protected by a layer of mucus, beneath it is **glandular tissue** with the gastric glands that make hydrochloric acid and the protease enzyme, and around the outside lie layers of **muscular tissue**. Because several tissues work together to carry out one specific function (digesting food), the stomach meets the definition of an organ, and you should always quote that reasoning in an exam answer.

bullets: **Glands** (salivary glands and pancreas) produce digestive juices containing enzymes.
**Stomach**: churns food, produces protease enzyme and hydrochloric acid.
**Liver**: produces bile.
**Small intestine**: produces enzymes and is where the digested food is absorbed into the blood.
**Large intestine**: absorbs water from the undigested food.
Together these organs digest food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood (full detail is in the next spec point).
core.p: The digestive system is the standard example of an organ system. It is an organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food. Reading the system from the bottom up shows all the levels: glandular cells make enzymes, which form glandular tissue, which together with muscular and epithelial tissue makes up the stomach (an organ), which is part of the digestive system, which is part of the human organism.

bullets: **Salivary glands** (near the mouth) make saliva containing the enzyme amylase.
**Oesophagus**: muscular tube that carries food to the stomach.
**Stomach**: churns food, makes protease enzyme and hydrochloric acid.
**Liver**: makes bile (stored in the gall bladder) which is released into the small intestine.
**Pancreas**: makes digestive enzymes (and insulin) and releases enzymes into the small intestine.
**Small intestine**: finishes digestion and absorbs the soluble food molecules into the blood.
**Large intestine**: absorbs water; the remaining waste (faeces) is stored in the rectum.
The path of food is a single tube from mouth to anus; the glands add juices to it but food does not pass through them.
core.h: The digestive system: where each organ is and what it does
core.p: The digestive system is the organ system you must be able to describe, and the AQA specification lists its parts as the glands (salivary glands and pancreas), the stomach, the liver, the small intestine and the large intestine. Food enters at the mouth, passes down the oesophagus into the stomach, then into the small intestine, then the large intestine, while digestive juices are added from the salivary glands, stomach, pancreas and liver (via bile stored in the gall bladder). Each organ is made of several tissues, so the system shows the whole chain: cells, tissues, organs, organ system. The system works with the circulatory system, which carries the absorbed small soluble molecules to every cell.

bullets: 1 cm cube: surface area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, SA:V = 6:1.
2 cm cube: surface area 24 cm², volume 8 cm³, SA:V = 3:1.
Surface area of a cube = 6 × side²; volume = side³; SA:V = 6 ÷ side, so it halves when the side doubles.
The small intestine has villi and the lungs have alveoli: both increase surface area for exchange.
The circulatory system carries materials quickly to cells deep inside the body, which diffusion alone could not do.
core.h: Why do large organisms need organisation? (SA:V)
core.p: A single-celled organism has a large surface area compared with its volume, so substances can simply diffuse in and out across the surface fast enough. As an organism gets bigger, its volume increases much faster than its surface area, so the **surface area to volume ratio falls**. Diffusion across the outer surface alone becomes far too slow to supply the inner cells. Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised **exchange surfaces** and **transport systems**, which means organs and organ systems.

bullets: Specialised cells arise by **differentiation** during development.
In animals most cells differentiate early and then cannot change; plant cells can differentiate throughout life.
Specialised cells being grouped into tissues makes the job more efficient and easier to control.
Efficiency gain: for example a whole stomach lining of glandular tissue makes far more enzyme than isolated cells could.
Disadvantage: damage to an organ can stop a whole system working (for example liver failure).
core.p: Organisation allows **division of labour**: each type of cell, tissue and organ concentrates on one job and does it very efficiently, instead of every cell doing everything. This is why multicellular organisms can be large and complex. The cost is that the parts depend on each other: if one tissue stops working properly the organ, system and organism may be affected.

bullets: Cell biology (4.1): specialised cells and their sub-cellular structures.
Enzymes and digestion (4.2.2): the stomach, pancreas, liver and small intestine.
Heart, blood vessels and blood (4.2.2): the circulatory system.
Plant tissues and organs (4.2.3): leaf, root, xylem, phloem, meristem.
Homeostasis (4.5): nervous and hormonal systems coordinate organ systems.
core.p: Organisation is the framework used for the whole of the rest of the biology course. Whenever you see a new organ, ask yourself: which tissues is it made of, what is its function, and which organ system is it part of? This habit lets you pick up marks in explanation questions quickly.

bullets: The **small intestine** needs muscular tissue (to push food along), glandular tissue (to make enzymes) and epithelial tissue (to absorb food).
The **pancreas** needs glandular tissue (to make digestive enzymes and insulin).
The **skin** needs epithelial tissue (covering), nervous tissue (sensation) and glandular tissue (sweat glands).
Always link the structure of the tissue to the function of the organ in your answer.
State the level correctly: a 'tissue' made of different cell types is wrong; that would be an organ.
core.h: Extension (Higher tier): applying the levels to unfamiliar organs
core.p: Higher-tier questions often give an unfamiliar organ and ask you to work out which tissues it must contain and why. The method is to look at what the organ has to do (its function) and then name the tissue that would do each part: movement means muscular tissue, secreting a substance means glandular tissue, covering a surface means epithelial tissue, sending signals means nervous tissue, and transport means vascular or blood tissue.

exam: Command word 'Name' or 'State' (1 mark): give the term only, for example 'organ system'. Do not add explanation unless asked.
'Describe the levels of organisation' (2 to 3 marks): list in the right order and link them: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, which form the organism.
'Define tissue / organ' (1 to 2 marks): use the exact wording; tissue = similar cells, similar function; organ = different tissues, specific function.
'Give the function of the muscular / glandular / epithelial tissue in the stomach' (1 mark each): churns food; makes enzymes and acid; covers the surfaces.
'Explain why the stomach is an organ' (2 marks): it is made of several different tissues (1) that work together to carry out a specific function, digesting food (1).

'Explain why large organisms need organ systems' (3 to 4 marks): smaller SA:V (1), diffusion too slow / distances too large (1), need exchange surfaces and transport systems (1), organs do this efficiently (1).
For SA:V calculation questions, show surface area, volume, then ratio; write the ratio as x : 1 and include units for area and volume.
Labelled diagrams: use a ruler to draw label lines, touch the structure and use the exact terms.
In 6-mark digestive system questions use the pattern: organ, what it makes or does, why it matters.
Read data tables carefully: pick the answer for the level that is asked (cell, tissue, organ or system).
Draw or label a diagram (3 to 4 marks): label the organ, point the line at the exact layer or structure, and use AQA terms (epithelial, glandular, muscular tissue; salivary gland, liver, pancreas).

mistakes.r: A tissue is a group of cells with a SIMILAR structure and function.
mistakes.w: A tissue is a group of different cells.

mistakes.r: An organ is an aggregation of different TISSUES working together to perform a specific function.
mistakes.w: An organ is a group of cells.

mistakes.r: The stomach is an organ because it is made of several tissues (muscular, glandular, epithelial).
The correct order is cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
mistakes.w: The levels are cell, organ, tissue, system.

mistakes.r: Organs work together in an organ system, and organ systems work together to form the organism.
Large organisms have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion alone is too slow and they need exchange surfaces and transport systems.
mistakes.w: Large organisms have bigger surface areas so exchange is easier.

mistakes.r: The stomach churns food (muscular tissue), makes protease and hydrochloric acid (glandular tissue) and is covered by epithelial tissue; the main absorption happens in the small intestine.
The glands are the salivary glands and the pancreas; the liver makes bile.
mistakes.w: Digestive glands are only the stomach.

mistakes.r: Food passes through the gut tube only; the liver and pancreas are glands that add juices (bile, enzymes) to the small intestine.
mistakes.w: Food passes through the liver and pancreas.

mistakes.r: Glandular tissue makes the enzymes and acid; muscular tissue churns the food.
mistakes.w: Muscular tissue in the stomach makes the enzymes.

summary: AQA requires you to know that cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms, that a tissue is a group of similar cells with a similar structure and function, that organs are aggregations of tissues performing specific functions, and that organs form organ systems which work together to make the organism. It matters because every later topic (digestion, circulation, gas exchange) is explained using these levels, and examiners test the definitions and the ability to apply them to a given example.

terms.d: The basic building block of all living organisms.
A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
An aggregation of tissues performing specific physiological functions.
A group of organs that work together to perform a particular function.
A whole living thing made of organ systems working together.
A cell whose structure is adapted to carry out a particular function.
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function.
Tissue that contracts to bring about movement.
Tissue that makes and secretes substances such as enzymes and hormones.
Tissue that covers the inside and outside surfaces of the body and organs.
An organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
An organ that produces and releases a substance such as a digestive juice or hormone.
A job carried out by part of a living organism.
The surface area of an organism divided by its volume; it decreases as organisms get larger.
A specialised surface with a large surface area where substances are exchanged with the environment.
An organ made of muscular, glandular and epithelial tissue that churns food and makes acid and protease.
A gland that makes digestive enzymes and releases them into the small intestine; it also makes insulin.
A gland near the mouth that makes saliva containing amylase.

worked.ans: SA:V = 1.5 : 1. As size increases the surface area to volume ratio decreases, so large organisms cannot rely on diffusion across their surface alone and need exchange surfaces and transport systems (organ systems).
worked.q: A 2 cm cube has a surface area to volume ratio of 3 : 1. Calculate the ratio for a 4 cm cube and explain what this shows about large organisms. (4 marks)
steps: As the cube doubles in size the ratio halves from 3:1 to 1.5:1.

worked.ans: Glandular cells make enzymes and similar cells form glandular tissue (1). Different tissues, such as muscular, glandular and epithelial, make up an organ such as the stomach (1). Several organs, such as the stomach, liver, pancreas and small intestine, work together in the digestive system to digest and absorb food (1).
worked.q: Describe how the levels of organisation are shown by the digestive system. (3 marks)
steps: Start with the smallest level and move upwards.
Use the digestive system for each level.
